lede: Stand a wheel on its edge, mark one spoke and turn it. The height of that mark rises and falls forever, and drawing that height against the angle gives the sine curve. Cosine is the same picture started at the top, and tangent is a third, stranger one.
can: Draw sin x, cos x and tan x over any part of -360 to 360 with their key points marked
State the period of each curve and use it to continue a graph
Read a second solution off the curve once your calculator has given you the first

md:
Stand a wheel on its edge, mark one spoke and turn it. The height of that mark rises and falls forever.
Plot that height against the angle turned and you get the sine curve. Everything in this topic is a fact about the shape of that picture, so the picture is what you learn.

alt: The graph of y = sin x from 0 to 360 degrees. It starts at the origin, rises to a maximum of 1 at 90 degrees, returns to 0 at 180 degrees, falls to a minimum of -1 at 270 degrees and comes back to 0 at 360 degrees.
caption: The sine curve, with the five points every sketch must show.

prompt: One tap to begin. Read the graph above: what is the greatest value $\sin x$ ever reaches?
explain: The curve tops out at $1$ and bottoms out at $-1$, and it never leaves that strip. That distance from the middle to the top is the amplitude, and on this specification it is always $1$, because the graphs are never stretched.

text: 1 Cosine: the same wave, started high

alt: The graph of y = cos x from 0 to 360 degrees. It starts at 1, falls to 0 at 90 degrees, reaches its minimum of -1 at 180 degrees, returns to 0 at 270 degrees and is back at 1 at 360 degrees.
caption: The cosine curve. Same shape, quarter of a turn earlier.

md:
Both curves come from the same turning point on the wheel: $\sin x$ is how far up it is, $\cos x$ is how far across.
At $0^\circ$ the spoke points straight out, so it is as far across as it can be and not up at all. That is why cosine starts at $1$ and sine starts at $0$.

title: Why the two curves are the same shape
md:
Turning the wheel a quarter turn swaps across for up, so the cosine curve is the sine curve slid a quarter period left. Every fact about one has a twin about the other.
That is also the trap: a sketch starting at the origin when the question said cosine is the wrong curve.

prompt: From the cosine graph, what is the value of $\cos 180^\circ$?
explain: The lowest point of the cosine curve sits at $180^\circ$, so the value there is $-1$. The sine curve is at its lowest at $270^\circ$ instead, which is the pair of facts worth keeping apart.

text: 2 Period: how far before it repeats

alt: The graph of y = sin x drawn from -360 to 360 degrees, showing three full waves, with the stretch from 0 to 360 degrees shaded and labelled one period.
caption: Sine repeats every $360^\circ$, so the shaded stretch is the whole story.

md:
One full turn of the wheel brings the spoke back where it started, so both $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ repeat every $360^\circ$. That number is the **period**.
Knowing it is how you extend a graph: whatever happens between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ happens again from $360^\circ$ to $720^\circ$, and happened before from $-360^\circ$ to $0^\circ$.

prompt: The sine curve is drawn for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$. At what angle, in degrees, does the next maximum after $90^\circ$ occur?
explain: Add one period: $90 + 360 = 450$. Every feature of the curve comes round again exactly $360^\circ$ later.

caption: Tangent has no maximum and no minimum; it has asymptotes instead.

md:
$\tan x$ is up divided by across. At $90^\circ$ the spoke points straight up, so across is zero and the division has no answer: the curve shoots off instead. Those are the **asymptotes**, drawn dashed at $x = 90^\circ$ and $x = 270^\circ$.
Between them the whole shape repeats after only $180^\circ$, so tangent's period is half of the other two.

prompt: Which of these does the tangent curve do at an asymptote?
options: It gets closer and closer without ever touching
It touches the line and turns back
It crosses the line at a steep angle
answer: It gets closer and closer without ever touching
explain: There is no value of $\tan x$ at $90^\circ$ at all, so there is nothing on the curve to touch the line with. A sketch whose curve meets an asymptote loses the mark for exactly that reason.

md:
**Worked sketch — $y = \cos x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.**
**1** Draw the axes and write $90$, $180$, $270$ and $360$ along the bottom and $1$ and $-1$ up the side, because the scale is a mark on its own.
**2** Plot the five points from the cosine column: $(0, 1)$, $(90, 0)$, $(180, -1)$, $(270, 0)$, $(360, 1)$.
**3** Join them with one smooth curve that is flat at the top and flat at the bottom. Straight sides between the turning points is the single commonest way this mark is lost.

prompt: You have plotted the five cosine points correctly and joined them with straight lines. What happens?
options: The points earn their mark and the shape mark is lost
answer: The points earn their mark and the shape mark is lost
explain: Examiners have reported this for several years running: the plotted values were right and the sides were too straight, so only the points were credited. One smooth pass with a pencil is all it takes.

md:
Solving $\sin x = 0.6$ in $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$ means finding where the curve reaches that height. Draw the line $y = 0.6$ across the graph and count the crossings: there are two.
A calculator gives you the first, $36.87^\circ$. The picture gives you the second, because it shows the curve coming back down to the same height on the other side of the maximum.

md:
The first arch of the sine curve is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$. So an angle $65^\circ$ short of the mirror pairs with one $65^\circ$ past it: $25^\circ$ pairs with $155^\circ$, and $\sin 25^\circ = \sin 155^\circ = 0.42$.
Written as a rule that is $\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin x$. Cosine and tangent each have their own version.

alt: A table of the three symmetry rules: sine mirrors about x = 90 so sin of 180 minus x equals sin x; cosine mirrors about x = 180 so cos of 360 minus x equals cos x; tangent has no mirror and simply repeats, so tan of x plus 180 equals tan x.

prompt: Given that $\cos 70^\circ = 0.34$, write down the value of $\cos 290^\circ$.
explain: $360 - 70 = 290$, and the cosine curve is symmetrical about $x = 180^\circ$, so the two heights are the same. Changing the sign would be a reflection in the x-axis, which is a different move altogether.

md:
Draw $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and $\tan x$ with their key points and scales marked.
State the period of each curve and use it to carry a graph further.
Draw the asymptotes of the tangent curve and say why the curve never reaches them.
Read the solutions of an equation off a curve by drawing a horizontal line.
Use the symmetry of a curve to turn one angle into a second one.

prompt: Before the reference panel, one check on the recap. Which pair of features is a sketch mark actually for?
options: The shape of the curve and the scale on the axes
The neatness of the pencil line and the size of the drawing
The number of points plotted and the colour used
answer: The shape of the curve and the scale on the axes
explain: Shape and scale are the two things the scheme names, and the key points are what the shape mark is judged against.

md: A trigonometric graph opens an early question for one or two marks: one for the shape, one for the scale or the key points. The part that follows is marked on your own sketch, so an accurate curve pays twice. If you cannot see the shape, plot the five key values first and join them last.
